external interrupt|hardware interrupt: Asynchronous interrupt from outside the CPU; examples: moving mouse, or pressing a key on the keyboard. See [External, internal and software interrupts](#/comp4736-p5/interrupt-classes).
internal interrupt|exception: Synchronous; "Generated by CPU itself whenever some unusual condition occurs"; example: 1/0. See [External, internal and software interrupts](#/comp4736-p5/interrupt-classes).
software interrupt|trap: Synchronous; examples: system calls. See [External, internal and software interrupts](#/comp4736-p5/interrupt-classes).
asynchronous / synchronous (interrupts): External (hardware) interrupts are asynchronous; internal interrupts (exceptions) and software interrupts (traps) are synchronous. See [External, internal and software interrupts](#/comp4736-p5/interrupt-classes).
two main functions of an operating syste: "Providing abstractions to user programs and managing the computer's resources". See [The system-call interface and the procedure library](#/comp4736-p5/system-call-interface).
system call: The set of calls the OS provides "that is an interface between the operating system and the user programs"; they vary from OS to OS and are highly machine dependent (slide 2); "the mechanism by which programs interact with the kernel of an operating system". See [Blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O](#/comp4736-p5/blocking-io).
procedure library: Since system calls "often must be expressed in assembly code", "an OS provides a procedure library to make system calls from C programs and often from other languages as well". See [The system-call interface and the procedure library](#/comp4736-p5/system-call-interface).
man page section 2: "System calls (functions provided by the kernel)"; section 1 is "Executable programs or shell commands", 3 "Library calls", 8 "System administration commands (usually only for root)"; the number in parentheses, e.g. FORK(2), LS(1), SUDO(8), is the section. See [The system-call interface and the procedure library](#/comp4736-p5/system-call-interface).
standard input|stdin|fd 0: Symbol `<`, fd 0, keyboard or file; e.g. `cat < myfile.txt`. See [stdin, stdout, stderr: file descriptors 0, 1, 2](#/comp4736-p5/standard-streams).
standard output|stdout|fd 1: Symbol `1>`, fd 1, terminal or file; e.g. `cat 1> myfile.txt` or `cat > myfile.txt`. See [stdin, stdout, stderr: file descriptors 0, 1, 2](#/comp4736-p5/standard-streams).
standard error|stderr|fd 2: Symbol `2>`, fd 2, terminal or file; e.g. `cat myfile 2> log_error`. See [stdin, stdout, stderr: file descriptors 0, 1, 2](#/comp4736-p5/standard-streams).
x86 register sizes: 8 bit A, B, C, D; 16 bit AX, BX, CX, DX; 32 bit EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX; 64 bit RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX; "AX = 0000h(16 bits)". See [x86 registers, int 80h and the syscall table](#/comp4736-p5/registers-and-int80).
EAX: On x86 Linux holds the system call number, and "The result, usually returned in the EAX register". See [x86 registers, int 80h and the syscall table](#/comp4736-p5/registers-and-int80).
EBX, ECX|argument registers: "Arguments to the system call : registers EBX, ECX, etc." (EDX third). See [x86 registers, int 80h and the syscall table](#/comp4736-p5/registers-and-int80).
int 80h|int 0x80: "Invoke the relevant interrupt (e.g. 80h is used for kernel call)"; `int 0x80 ;call kernel` (slides 11-12); i386 instruction `int $0x80` in man syscall. See [x86 registers, int 80h and the syscall table](#/comp4736-p5/registers-and-int80).
syscall number|system-call number: The number identifying the call, placed in EAX on x86 (sys_exit 1, sys_fork 2, sys_read 3, sys_write 4, sys_open 5, sys_close 6) (slide 11); the library procedure "puts the system-call number in a place where the operating system expects it, such as a register" (slide 19); on x86_64 read 0, write 1, open 2, close 3. See [x86 registers, int 80h and the syscall table](#/comp4736-p5/registers-and-int80).
sys_write / sys_exit (x86): Eax 4 with ebx = fd, ecx = buffer, edx = length; eax 1 with ebx = int status. See [x86 registers, int 80h and the syscall table](#/comp4736-p5/registers-and-int80).
syscall (x86-64 / MIPS instruction): The x86-64 kernel-entry instruction, number in rax, args rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9 (slides 14-15); MIPS `syscall` with service in $v0 (15 = write to file; $a0 fd, $a1 buffer address, $a2 count). See [x86 registers, int 80h and the syscall table](#/comp4736-p5/registers-and-int80).
syscall() library function: "a small library function that invokes the system call whose assembly language interface has the specified number with the specified arguments. Employing syscall() is useful, for example, when invoking a system call that has no wrapper function in the C library". See [x86 registers, int 80h and the syscall table](#/comp4736-p5/registers-and-int80).
vdso: Referred to in man syscall: the trap instruction "might not be the fastest or best way to transition to the kernel, so you might have to refer to vdso(7)". See [x86 registers, int 80h and the syscall table](#/comp4736-p5/registers-and-int80).
ausyscall --dump: Prints the syscall table ("Using x86_64 syscall table: 0 read, 1 write, 2 open, 3 close …"). See [x86 registers, int 80h and the syscall table](#/comp4736-p5/registers-and-int80).
TRAP instruction: Step 6, executed "to switch from user mode to kernel mode and start execution at a fixed address within the kernel". See [The eleven steps of read(fd, buffer, nbytes)](#/comp4736-p5/eleven-steps).
system-call handler: The kernel code following the TRAP "dispatches to the correct system-call handler, usually via a table of pointers to system-call handlers indexed on system-call number" (step 7); "At that point the system-call handler runs" (step 8). See [The eleven steps of read(fd, buffer, nbytes)](#/comp4736-p5/eleven-steps).
11 steps of read(fd, buffer, nbytes): 1-3 push parameters in reverse order; 4 call library procedure; 5 put syscall number in register; 6 TRAP to kernel; 7 dispatch via table; 8 handler runs; 9 return to library procedure after the TRAP; 10 return to user program; 11 user program cleans up the stack (Increment SP). See [The eleven steps of read(fd, buffer, nbytes)](#/comp4736-p5/eleven-steps).
user space / kernel space: In the read figure, user space holds the user program and library procedure read; kernel space (operating system) holds Dispatch, the table and the Sys call handler; addresses run 0 to 0xFFFFFFFF. See [The eleven steps of read(fd, buffer, nbytes)](#/comp4736-p5/eleven-steps).
POSIX return codes: "The return code s is −1 if an error has occurred"; pid is a process id, fd is a file descriptor, n is a byte count, position is an offset within the file, seconds is the elapsed time. See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
fork|pid = fork( ): "Create a child process identical to the parent" (slide 22); man: "fork - create a child process", `pid_t fork(void);`. See [The system-call interface and the procedure library](#/comp4736-p5/system-call-interface).
fork return value −1: "pid=-1 fork fails". See [fork returns three ways: every slide program and its output](#/comp4736-p5/fork-programs).
fork return value 0: "pid=0 return value in the child process". See [fork returns three ways: every slide program and its output](#/comp4736-p5/fork-programs).
fork return value > 0: "pid>0 return value in the parent process (returns the process ID of the child process to the parent process)". See [fork returns three ways: every slide program and its output](#/comp4736-p5/fork-programs).
successful fork: "(fork()≥0): Execution in both the parent and child process continues at the instruction following the fork". See [fork returns three ways: every slide program and its output](#/comp4736-p5/fork-programs).
waitpid|pid = waitpid(pid, &statloc, opt: "Wait for a child to terminate" (slide 22); `waitpid(-1, &status, 0)` waits for a child. See [fork returns three ways: every slide program and its output](#/comp4736-p5/fork-programs).
execve|s = execve(name, argv, environp): "Replace a process' core image" (slide 22); man: "execve - execute program"; "executes the program referred to by pathname. This causes the program that is currently being run by the calling process to be replaced with a new program, with newly initialized stack, heap, and data segments"; `int execve(const char *pathname, char *const argv[], char *const envp[]);`. See [execve, the shell loop, and why "Error" never prints](#/comp4736-p5/execve-and-the-shell).
exec family|execl, execlp, execle, execv: EXEC(3) "execute a file" (library calls, section 3). See [execve, the shell loop, and why "Error" never prints](#/comp4736-p5/execve-and-the-shell).
exit|exit(status): "Terminate process execution and return status". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
stripped-down shell: Loop forever: type_prompt, read_command, `if (fork() != 0)` parent `waitpid(−1, &status, 0)`, else child `execve(command, parameters, 0)`; "TRUE is assumed to be defined as 1". See [execve, the shell loop, and why "Error" never prints](#/comp4736-p5/execve-and-the-shell).
open|fd = open(file, how, ...): "Open a file for reading, writing, or both". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
close|s = close(fd): "Close an open file". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
read|n = read(fd, buffer, nbytes): "Read data from a file into a buffer". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
write|n = write(fd, buffer, nbytes): "Write data from a buffer into a file". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
lseek|position = lseek(fd, offset, whenc: "Move the file pointer". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
stat|s = stat(name, &buf): "Get a file's status information". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
mkdir|s = mkdir(name, mode): "Create a new directory". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
rmdir|s = rmdir(name): "Remove an empty directory". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
link|s = link(name1, name2): "Create a new entry, name2, pointing to name1" (slide 40); `link("/usr/jim/memo", "/usr/ast/note")` adds entry "70 note" to /usr/ast, same i-number 70 as memo. See [link, hard and symbolic links, mount](#/comp4736-p5/links-and-mount).
unlink|s = unlink(name): "Remove a directory entry". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
mount|s = mount(special, name, flag): "Mount a file system" (slide 40); "the mount system call allows two file systems to be merged into one". See [link, hard and symbolic links, mount](#/comp4736-p5/links-and-mount).
umount|s = umount(special): "Unmount a file system". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
chdir|s = chdir(dirname): "Change the working directory". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
chmod|s = chmod(name, mode): "Change a file's protection bits". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
kill|s = kill(pid, signal): "Send a signal to a process". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
time|seconds = time(&seconds): "Get the elapsed time since Jan. 1, 1970". See [The POSIX system calls and what they return](#/comp4736-p5/posix-tables).
i-number|inode: The number beside each name in a directory (e.g. 16 mail, 70 memo); two names with the same i-number are the same file (slide 42); stat shows "Inode:". See [link, hard and symbolic links, mount](#/comp4736-p5/links-and-mount).
hard link: A second directory entry for the same file: same inode, "regular file", same size; my_file and my_file_h_link both point directly at the data. See [link, hard and symbolic links, mount](#/comp4736-p5/links-and-mount).
link count|Links: "# of links to the main file"; 2 for my_file with one hard link, drops to 1 after my_file is deleted. See [link, hard and symbolic links, mount](#/comp4736-p5/links-and-mount).
symbolic link: A separate file (own inode, type "symbolic link", Size 7, Blocks 0, Links 1, mode lrwxrwxrwx) that points to the name my_file, not the data (slides 44-45); after my_file is deleted, `cat my_file_s_link` gives "No such file or directory" while the hard link still reads. See [link, hard and symbolic links, mount](#/comp4736-p5/links-and-mount).
CreateProcess: Win32 for fork; "Create a new process"; "CreateProcess = fork + execve". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
WaitForSingleObject: Win32 for waitpid; "Can wait for a process to exit". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
ExitProcess: Win32 for exit; "Terminate execution". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
CreateFile: Win32 for open; "Create a file or open an existing file". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
CloseHandle: Win32 for close; "Close a file". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
ReadFile: Win32 for read; "Read data from a file". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
WriteFile: Win32 for write; "Write data to a file". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
SetFilePointer: Win32 for lseek; "Move the file pointer". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
GetFileAttributesEx: Win32 for stat; "Get various file attributes". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
CreateDirectory: Win32 for mkdir; "Create a new directory". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
RemoveDirectory: Win32 for rmdir; "Remove an empty directory". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
DeleteFile: Win32 for unlink; "Destroy an existing file". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
SetCurrentDirectory: Win32 for chdir; "Change the current working directory". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
GetLocalTime: Win32 for time; "Get the current time". See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
(none) in Win32: Execve (CreateProcess = fork + execve), link ("Win32 does not support links"), mount and umount ("Win32 does not support mount"), chmod ("Win32 does not support security (although NT does)"), kill ("Win32 does not support signals"). See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
strace: "trace system calls and signals"; `-c --summary-only` "Count time, calls, and errors for each system call and report a summary on program exit, suppressing the regular output"; a hello-world program made 33 calls, 2 errors. See [The Win32 API against UNIX, and strace](#/comp4736-p5/win32-api).
blocking system call: "suspends the execution of the process until the operation is completed"; "Most I/O system calls, by default, are blocking calls"; e.g. `open("file.txt", O_RDONLY)`. See [Blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O](#/comp4736-p5/blocking-io).
non-blocking system call: "returns immediately, even if the requested operation hasn't been completed. Instead of waiting, the program continues executing other code while periodically checking if the operation has finished". See [Blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O](#/comp4736-p5/blocking-io).
fcntl: "To enable non-blocking mode, you often use the fcntl system call to modify the file descriptor": `fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, O_NONBLOCK);`. See [Blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O](#/comp4736-p5/blocking-io).
O_NONBLOCK: Flag set via fcntl or passed to open (`O_RDONLY | O_NONBLOCK`); man note: "this flag has no effect for regular files and block devices". See [Blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O](#/comp4736-p5/blocking-io).
POSIX AIO|POSIX Asynchronous I/O: "provides another method of non-blocking I/O where you can initiate I/O operations and have them complete asynchronously, i.e., in the background. This allows a program to perform other tasks while waiting for the operation to complete". See [Blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O](#/comp4736-p5/blocking-io).
aio_read, aio_write, aio_error, aio_retu: Functions that "enable asynchronous operations"; `aio_read(&cb); // Asynchronous read call`. See [Blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O](#/comp4736-p5/blocking-io).
struct aiocb: AIO control block; fields set in the example: aio_fildes = fd, aio_buf = buffer, aio_nbytes = sizeof(buffer), aio_offset = 0. See [Blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O](#/comp4736-p5/blocking-io).
blocking I/O vs non-blocking I/O: Blocking: simpler code flow, easier where performance or responsiveness isn't critical, execution pauses until I/O completes; non-blocking: prevents stalling, needs more complex logic (checking completion or event loops), useful for responsive apps (GUIs, network servers). See [Blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O](#/comp4736-p5/blocking-io).
